Globe vs Flat Earth: what this page does

Two models of the Earth, side by side: the Globe Earth (GE) and the Flat Earth (FE) on the Gleason map. Pick any place and time and each model draws the sky it predicts: the Sun, the Moon, the stars and the horizon. The table under the views lists each prediction next to the real sky, so you can see which model matches. Better still, step outside and compare with what you observe.

How each model is built

  • Real sky: Astronomy Engine, an ephemeris that matches telescope observations to well under 1 arc-minute, including the bending of light by the air.
  • Globe: plain sphere geometry, directly computed in this page. The Sun is the only light, so day, night, Moon phases and eclipses come out by themselves.
  • Flat: given its strongest version. It uses the real point on Earth under the Sun and Moon, and places both 4,828 km (3,000 miles) above the Gleason map, each 51 km wide. Night assumes the Flat-Earth Sun is a "spotlight": it is dark more than about 10,000 km from the point under the Sun (adjustable). Stars sit on a dome (the "firmament") 10,000 km high over the North Pole that comes down at the "Ice Wall" in Antarctica. You can change these figures in Flat model settings.

Short names in the views: GE means Globe Earth and FE means Flat Earth. FE Sun and FE Moon are the flat model's own Sun and Moon. On the flat view, the red and blue circles labelled GE Sun and GE Moon show where the real Sun and Moon are, as the globe model predicts.

Horizon: the air bends light slightly round the curve, so the real horizon is about 7% farther than plain geometry gives. On a flat disc there would be no horizon at all, only haze.

This page is free, with no ads and no tracking. If you would like to help future work, such as a phone app, you can support it on Ko-fi.

Stars: the 520 brightest (magnitude 4 and above) from the Hipparcos catalogue, with lines for 18 constellations, via d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD). Earth images: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble. Moon map: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

Options

Top bar

Model
Both models side by side, or one alone, full width.
View
Observer: what you would see standing there. Space: the whole planet from outside.
Scale
Enlarged makes the Sun and Moon visible in Space view. True shows real sizes and distances.
Stars
Off, on, with names, or Trails: the paths stars draw across the sky during playback.
Solar filter
Removes the Sun's glare so you can see its disc, for example during an eclipse.
Labels
Shows or hides the names on the views.
km | mi (top right)
Shows distances, altitudes and speeds in kilometres or in miles (feet for low altitudes, mph for speeds).
EN | FR (top right)
Switches the whole page between English and French.

Left panel

Observer
Choose a place, type coordinates, or set the altitude from the ground up to space. Face buttons turn the view toward the Sun, Moon, Polaris or the Southern Cross; Follow keeps it there.
Saved places
Keep your own locations in this browser.
Date and time
Any date, in the time zone you choose (yours by default), with playback at several speeds. Real events jumps to famous eclipses and observations.
Distance
The distance between two cities on each model.
Real flight routes
Real flights with their actual flight times, and the speed each model would need.
Flat model settings
Try other heights and sizes for the FE Sun, Moon and firmament, and other sizes for the Sun's spotlight.

Mouse: drag to look around (or to orbit in Space view), scroll to zoom. In Space view, or from 2,000 km up, click any point on the planet to go there. Each section of the left panel folds when you click its title.

Observer

Observer view: drag to look around, scroll to zoom. From 2,000 km up, or in Space view, click any point to go there. Space view: drag to orbit.

Saved places

    Click any point on a full-planet view (Space view, or 2,000 km and higher) to pick it, then save it here.

    Real flight routes

    Tick a route to see its distance, real flight time and the speed it needs on each model.

    Lines follow the great-circle route. On the flat map the same route bends into long arcs.

    Flat model settings

    Flat-earthers never agree on these numbers, so try your own. The defaults are the usual claims: Sun and Moon 51 km wide, 4,828 km (3,000 miles) up.
